a: harm will not lay hold of you
p: The Greek uses one word for the evil you do and the harm that comes back.
b: The Greek repeats kakos: do not do kaka (evil things), and kakon (evil, harm) will not seize you. English needs two words, "evil" and "harm," but the Greek ties them together: what you send out is what comes back. The Hebrew, as Kahana prints it, has the same repetition: אַל תַּעַשׂ רָעָה וְאַל יַשִּׂיגְךָ רָעָה. This chapter begins a long run of short commands that start "Do not" (Greek mē), the style of a teacher drilling his students.
orig: καὶ οὐ μή σε καταλάβῃ κακόν (kai ou mē se katalabē kakon), "and evil will never seize you"

p: Ben Sira speaks as a teacher to a pupil, the way Proverbs does.
b: Here the Greek has huie, "son"; at 10:28 and 11:10 it has teknon, "child," which this site renders "my child." Both stand for the Hebrew beni, "my son," the form of address of a teacher to his pupil, as in Proverbs 1:8 and Proverbs 6:1. The Hebrew of Kahana uses beni at 10:28 and 11:10 (Kahana 10:28; 11:11) but not here. Ben Sira taught young men in Jerusalem (51:23 calls his school a "house of instruction"), so "son" is a pupil as much as a child. The address includes daughters only by later application; the advice on wives and daughters in 7:19-26 and chapter 9 shows the pupils were men.
orig: υἱέ (huie), "son"

p: The farmer's image of sowing and reaping wrong is old in Israel's wisdom and prophets.
b: Proverbs says it plainly: "Plant wrongdoing and you will harvest disaster" (Proverbs 22:8). Hosea accuses Israel: "You plowed wickedness. / You harvested injustice" (Hosea 10:13), and Job's friend Eliphaz had seen that those who plow trouble reap it (Job 4:8). Paul uses the same picture for the life of the Spirit: "Whatever a person sows, that is what he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). "Seven times over" means in full measure, as in Genesis 4:15 and Proverbs 6:31.
r: Proverbs 22:8; Hosea 10:13; Job 4:8; Galatians 6:7; Genesis 4:15; Proverbs 6:31

p: Ben Sira warns his pupils, who were trained for public life, against hunting for power.
b: Scribes in Ben Sira's Jerusalem served rulers and sat in councils (8:8; 39:4), so the temptation to seek office was real for his students. The warning is not that office is evil but that a person may not be strong enough for it (7:6). The Greek hēgemonia is leadership or command; the Hebrew in Kahana has memshelet, "rule." Compare Jesus' warning not to grab the place of honor at a feast (Luke 14:8-11).
orig: ἡγεμονίαν (hēgemonian), "leadership, command"

a: Do not claim to be in the right before the Lord
t: No one is in the right before God
p: Ben Sira agrees with Job, the Psalms and Paul that no one can stand on his own record before God.
b: The Greek verb dikaioō, "declare righteous, justify," here in the middle voice, means "do not justify yourself." The thought matches the 66 books: "How can a human be in the right before God?" (Job 9:2), and the psalmist's plea, "no one living is righteous before you" (Psalm 143:2). Jesus told of a Pharisee who listed his virtues and a tax collector who only begged for mercy, and said the second went home justified (Luke 18:9-14). Ben Sira draws no doctrine of justification from it; his point is humility.
orig: μὴ δικαιοῦ ἔναντι Κυρίου (mē dikaiou enanti Kyriou), "do not justify yourself before the Lord"

t: A trap for your own honesty
p: A judge who fears the powerful trips up his own integrity.
b: The Greek skandalon is the trigger of a trap, then anything that makes a person fall; it is the word the New Testament uses for a "stumbling block" (Matthew 18:7; Romans 14:13). A judge who is afraid of a powerful man will bend his ruling, and so he sets a trap in the path of his own "uprightness" (euthytēs, straightness). The Law forbids a judge to favor the great (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 1:17). The Hebrew in Kahana is different: "and put a bribe in your integrity."
orig: θήσεις σκάνδαλον (thēseis skandalon), "you will set a stumbling block"

p: The Greek pictures sins tied together in a bundle.
b: The verb katadesmeuō means to bind fast. "Do not bind a sin twice" means do not repeat a sin, or add a second sin to the first, for even the first one brings guilt. The Hebrew in Kahana uses tiqshor, "tie," the same picture. Someone later wrote this verse again in the margin of Codex Vaticanus at 12:12, as Swete's notes show, perhaps as a fitting comment there.
orig: μὴ καταδεσμεύσῃς δὶς ἁμαρτίαν (mē katadesmeusēs dis hamartian), "do not bind a sin twice"

a: He will notice how many gifts I bring
p: Ben Sira shares the prophets' warning that offerings do not cover a wrong life.
b: The man Ben Sira quotes thinks the size of his offerings will make God overlook his sins. The 66 books say the same as Ben Sira: "When the wicked sacrifice, the LORD finds it abhorrent" (Proverbs 15:8), and Isaiah has God refuse a multitude of sacrifices from hands full of blood (Isaiah 1:11-15). Ben Sira returns to this later, on the offerings of the unjust (31:21-27 in the Greek order, 34:18-22 in the KJV) and the sacrifice of keeping the law (32:1-26 Greek, chapter 35 KJV). He is not against sacrifice: in 7:29-31 he tells his pupils to give the priests their full share.

p: Ben Sira often calls God "the Most High," a title as old as Genesis.
b: The Greek hypsistos, "highest," stands for the Hebrew Elyon. Melchizedek blesses Abram by "God Most High" (Genesis 14:19), and the title is common in the Psalms. Ben Sira uses it often (7:15; 9:15; 12:2, 6). The Greek of Sirach has no divine name: Kyrios is "the Lord," never "the LORD," because the translator, like all Greek translators, put Kyrios where the Hebrew had the name.
orig: θεῷ ὑψίστῳ (theō hypsistō), "to God Most High"

p: The Greek says "alms"; the Hebrew says tsedaqah, "righteousness," the later Jewish word for charity.
b: The Greek eleēmosynē, from eleos, "mercy," means a gift to the poor. The Hebrew in Kahana has וּבִצְדָקָה אַל תִּתְעַבָּר, "and in tsedaqah do not be wanting." In the Bible tsedaqah is "righteousness," but in Ben Sira and later Hebrew it also means charity, giving to the poor, as it still does in Jewish life. Ben Sira pairs prayer with almsgiving, as Tobit does (Tobit 12:8) and as Jesus does in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:1-6).
orig: ἐλεημοσύνην (eleēmosynēn), "alms, mercy shown to the poor"

a: there is One who brings low and lifts high
t: The God who brings low and lifts up
p: Hannah's song and Mary's song both praise the God who reverses people's fortunes.
b: Hannah sang, "he puts them down, and he also raises them up" (1 Samuel 2:7), and Mary sang, "He has pulled rulers down from thrones / and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52). Ben Sira draws a practical lesson: since God can turn things around, do not mock a person in bitter trouble, for tomorrow you may be the one laid low. The theme returns in 10:14-15 and 11:5-6, 12-13.

p: Both the Greek and the Hebrew use a farming verb for making up lies.
b: The Greek arotriaō means "to plow"; the Hebrew in Kahana has tacharosh, "plow, devise." In Hebrew the verb charash means both to plow and to plot (Proverbs 3:29; Proverbs 6:14), and the Greek translator kept the farmer's image instead of turning it into plain "devise," as the KJV does. It follows the sowing of 7:3.
orig: μὴ ἀροτρία ψεῦδος (mē arotria pseudos), "do not plow a lie"

a: do not say the same words over and over when you pray
p: Jesus gives a similar warning about prayer in the Sermon on the Mount.
b: The Greek deuteroō means to do a second time, to repeat. Jesus said, "When you are praying, do not chatter on like the Gentiles. They imagine that all their talking will get them a hearing" (Matthew 6:7). Ecclesiastes advises, "let your words be few" before God (Ecclesiastes 5:2). Ben Sira links talk in prayer with talk in the council of elders: in both places, babbling is a lack of respect. This is a warning against empty words, not against praying often (Luke 18:1).
orig: μὴ δευτερώσῃς λόγον (mē deuterōsēs logon), "do not repeat a word"

a: farm work, which the Most High created
p: Ben Sira says farm work was created by God, a view rooted in Genesis.
b: In Genesis, God put the man in the garden "to work it and to keep it" (Genesis 2:15) before the curse made the work painful (Genesis 3:17-19). Ben Sira, a scribe who prized study (38:24-34), still tells his pupils not to look down on hard physical work. The Hebrew in Kahana puts this line earlier in the chapter and says the work "was allotted by God."

t: Fire and worm: punishment after death?
p: The Greek speaks of fire and the worm for the ungodly; the Hebrew speaks only of worms for every mortal.
b: The Greek line echoes Isaiah 66:24, "their worm will not die, / and their fire will not be put out," which Jesus quotes for Gehenna: "where their worm never dies and the fire is never put out" (Mark 9:48). Judith 16:17 also has "fire and worms" for God's enemies. But the Hebrew Ben Sira wrote, as Kahana prints it, says כִּי תִקְוַת אֱנוֹשׁ רִמָּה, "for the hope of mortal man is worms": all humans end in the grave, so be humble. The Greek may show how the grandson, translating in Egypt after 132 BC, understood the line, or it may come from a Hebrew copy unlike the one that survives; see the variant on this verse. Elsewhere Ben Sira says that no one in Hades praises the Most High (17:27) and that "in Hades there is no questioning about life" (41:4), so he does not build a doctrine of punishment after death on this line.

p: Ophir was the land of the finest gold; the Greek spells it Souphir.
b: The Greek has Soupheir. The Greek Old Testament spells the place in several ways (Sōphēra in 1 Kings 9:28, Sōpheira in 2 Chronicles 8:18). Ophir was the far-off land (perhaps in Arabia, Africa or India) where Solomon's ships fetched gold (1 Kings 9:28; 1 Kings 10:11). "Gold of Ophir" was proverbial for the best gold (Job 22:24; Job 28:16; Psalm 45:9). The Hebrew in Kahana has zehav Ophir, "gold of Ophir." A true friend is worth more than the best gold, as a good wife is in the next verse.
orig: χρυσίῳ Σουφείρ (chrysiō Soupheir), "gold of Souphir"

p: The Greek says "for something indifferent"; the Hebrew says "for a price."
b: The Greek adiaphoros means something that makes no difference, of no account. The Hebrew in Kahana reads bimchir, "for a price": do not sell a friend for money. Either way the point is the worth of a friend, a theme Ben Sira treats at length in chapter 6 (6:5-17) and again in 9:10 and 12:8-9.
orig: ἕνεκεν ἀδιαφόρου (heneken adiaphorou), "for the sake of something indifferent"

p: Ben Sira echoes Proverbs: a good wife is a treasure beyond price.
b: Proverbs says, "The one who finds a wife has found something good, / and he draws favor from the LORD" (Proverbs 18:22), and asks, "A woman of strength, who can find one? / Her price is far beyond red coral" (Proverbs 31:10). The Hebrew in Kahana says her charm is worth more than peninim, the same precious stones (or corals) of Proverbs 31:10; the Greek says "gold," picking up the gold of the verse before. Ben Sira returns to wives in 9:1-2, chapters 25-26 and 36:23-31 (Greek numbering).
orig: γυναικὸς σοφῆς καὶ ἀγαθῆς (gynaikos sophēs kai agathēs), "a wise and good woman (wife)"

a: do not hold back his freedom
p: The "servant" here is a household slave, and Ben Sira urges giving him his freedom.
b: The Greek oiketēs is a household servant, usually a slave, and eleutheria is freedom, release from slavery. The Law of Moses set a Hebrew slave free in the seventh year: "In the seventh he goes free, owing nothing" (Exodus 21:2; compare Deuteronomy 15:12-15). Jeremiah condemned the rich of Jerusalem who freed their slaves and then took them back (Jeremiah 34:8-17). The Hebrew in Kahana reads "love a wise slave like yourself." Ben Sira assumes slavery, as his whole world did; here he urges kindness and release. At 30:33-40 (Greek numbering; 33:24-31 in the KJV) he gives harsher advice about slaves.
orig: μὴ στερήσῃς αὐτὸν ἐλευθερίας (mē sterēsēs auton eleutherias), "do not deprive him of freedom"

p: Ben Sira follows Proverbs' practical advice on caring for animals.
b: Proverbs says, "Make sure you know the faces of your sheep; / set your heart on your herds" (Proverbs 27:23). The Greek episkeptou means "look after, watch over," the same verb used for visiting the sick in 7:35. Verses 22-26 run through a household: animals, sons, daughters, wife, the way the household codes of the New Testament later run through wives, children and slaves (Colossians 3:18-4:1).
orig: ἐπισκέπτου αὐτά (episkeptou auta), "look after them"

p: The Greek paideuō covers both teaching and correcting; this part renders it "instruct."
b: The verb paideuō (noun paideia) means to bring up a child, to train, teach and correct. English has no single word for all of it. In this part of the Plain it is "instruct" (8:8; 10:1) and the person without it is "untaught" (8:4; 10:3). "Bend their necks" shows that correction is meant too, as in Proverbs: "one who loves him seeks him out early with discipline" (Proverbs 13:24). The Hebrew in Kahana has a different second line: "and take wives for them in their youth." See the variant on this verse.
orig: παίδευσον αὐτά (paideuson auta), "instruct them, train them"

a: do not turn a beaming face toward them
p: The Greek idiom means not to be too easy on a daughter.
b: Literally "do not make your face cheerful toward them." The Hebrew in Kahana reads "do not make your face shine on them," the language of favor (Numbers 6:25). Ben Sira wants a father to be strict and watchful with his daughters, because a daughter's honor, and her family's, depended on her chastity before marriage (Deuteronomy 22:13-21). He comes back to a father's worry over daughters in 42:9-14, a passage the Talmud quotes (Sanhedrin 100b). This is the advice of a man of his time; the Plain does not soften it.
orig: μὴ ἱλαρώσῃς πρὸς αὐτὰς τὸ πρόσωπόν σου (mē hilarōsēs pros autas to prosōpon sou)

p: To "drive out" a wife meant to divorce her.
b: The Greek ekballō, "throw out," is the language of divorce: a husband sent his wife out of his house (Deuteronomy 24:1). Ben Sira tells a man who has a wife he loves not to divorce her. Malachi says the LORD hates divorce (Malachi 2:16), and Jesus forbade it (Mark 10:2-12). Some Greek copies and the Hebrew add a second line about a wife who is hated; see the variant.
orig: μὴ ἐκβάλῃς αὐτήν (mē ekbalēs autēn), "do not throw her out"

a: Honor your father with all your heart
p: Ben Sira restates the commandment and gives a reason: remember your mother's labor.
b: The command is the fifth (in Catholic and Lutheran counting the fourth) of the Ten Commandments: "Honor your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12). Ben Sira has already taught on it at length in 3:1-16. Here he adds the reason of gratitude: they gave you life, and you can never pay them back (7:28). The Catholic Catechism quotes 7:27-28 for this very point (see the chapter page). The Hebrew of 7:27-28 is in brackets in Kahana: his own reconstruction, not manuscript text.

p: Verses 29-30 echo Deuteronomy 6:5, "with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength."
b: The great commandment says, "Love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength" (Deuteronomy 6:5). The Greek of 7:29-30 says "with all your soul" and "with all your strength" (dynamis, the word of the Greek Deuteronomy 6:5). The Hebrew in Kahana has "with all your heart" (7:29) and "with all your might," בְּכָל מְאֹדְךָ (bekhol me'odekha), the exact word of Deuteronomy 6:5. Ben Sira takes the love owed to God and applies it to the honor owed to his priests. Jesus called this the first commandment (Mark 12:29-30).

p: Ben Sira lists the portions the Law gives the priests.
b: The list follows the Law: the "guilt offering" (Leviticus 5:14-6:7; Leviticus 7:1-7), whose meat went to the priests; "the gift of the shoulders," the foreleg the priest received from every sacrifice (Deuteronomy 18:3, "the foreleg," Greek brachiona, the word used here), and the right thigh of peace offerings (Leviticus 7:32-34); "the sacrifice of consecration," probably the offerings that set things apart as holy; and "the first fruits" (Numbers 18:12-13; Deuteronomy 26:1-11). Priests had no land of their own and lived on these gifts (Numbers 18:20). Ben Sira admired the priests, above all the high priest Simon (chapter 50).
orig: δόσιν βραχιόνων (dosin brachionōn), "a gift of shoulders (forelegs)"

a: so your blessing will be made whole
p: Giving to the poor completes a person's religion after the offerings to the priest.
b: The Greek teleioō means to complete, to make perfect. After the gifts to the priests (7:31), Ben Sira says your blessing is not complete until you also open your hand to the poor. Deuteronomy commands: "open your hand wide to your brother, to the poor and needy" (Deuteronomy 15:11). The Hebrew in Kahana reads tishlam, "may be complete."
orig: ἵνα τελειωθῇ ἡ εὐλογία σου (hina teleiōthē hē eulogia sou)

a: do not keep your kindness from the dead
p: What kindness is owed the dead? Burial and mourning at least; some read more into it.
b: The Greek charis is grace, favor, kindness; the Hebrew in Kahana has chesed, "loyal love": וְגַם מִמֵּת אַל תִּמְנַע חָסֶד. Naomi blessed the LORD, who "has not left off his loyal love to the living or the dead" (Ruth 2:20). The plainest reading is the duty to bury the dead and to mourn them, which Tobit risks his life to do (Tobit 1:17-18; Tobit 2:3-8), and the next verse turns to mourning. Some Christian readers have also seen here a duty of prayer for the dead, which other churches reject; that question is treated on the topic page for purgatory and at 2 Maccabees 12:43-45, which speaks of it directly.
orig: ἐπὶ νεκρῷ μὴ ἀποκωλύσῃς χάριν (epi nekrō mē apokōlysēs charin)

a: grieve along with those who grieve
p: Paul gives almost the same command in Romans.
b: Paul writes, "Be glad along with the glad. Weep along with those who weep" (Romans 12:15). The Greek of both passages joins the verb to "with" (meta here, meta in Romans 12:15 too). In Jewish practice, comforting mourners became one of the great works of kindness, beside visiting the sick (the next verse) and burying the dead (7:33).

p: Jesus counts visiting the sick as service done to him.
b: The Greek episkeptesthai means to look in on, to visit with care. Jesus says, "When I was sick, you took care of me" (Matthew 25:36), using the same verb, and James calls true religion "to visit orphans and widows in their trouble" (James 1:27). Later Jewish teaching counts visiting the sick (bikkur cholim) among the deeds of loving-kindness. The Hebrew line in Kahana reads differently and does not speak of the sick.
orig: ἐπισκέπτεσθαι ἄρρωστον (episkeptesthai arrōston), "to visit a sick person"

p: The Greek ta eschata, "the last things," became the Latin "memorare novissima tua."
b: The Greek ta eschata sou means "your last things," the end of your life. The Hebrew in Kahana has acharit, "end, outcome": בְּכָל מַעֲשֶׂיךָ זְכוֹר אַחֲרִית, "in all your deeds remember the end." Moses wished that Israel would "understand their end" (Deuteronomy 32:29), and the psalmist prays to be taught to number his days (Psalm 90:12). In the Latin Vulgate this verse is 7:40: "memorare novissima tua," "remember your last things." Ben Sira means death; Christian readers later heard in "the last things" death, judgment, heaven and hell.
orig: μιμνήσκου τὰ ἔσχατά σου (mimnēskou ta eschata sou), "remember your last things"
